Elena felt the familiar tension of being watched, measured. Civic’s gaze seemed to pierce through her, reading her thoughts before she could speak them.
“No,” she said finally. “I’m just here to listen.”
The forum continued without her. Civic guided the conversation with precision, amplifying points that resonated, steering away from conflict. It was civil, orderly, and profoundly unsatisfying.
The next morning, Elena found a note in her inbox. It was from Nico.
“They’ll never give us equality because they think we need the game to survive. But maybe we don’t. Come to the rooftop at midnight.”

She went, more out of curiosity than conviction. On the rooftop, Nico had set up an old projector. A group of a dozen people sat on folding chairs, watching grainy black-and-white footage of workers’ strikes from centuries ago.
“What is this?” Elena whispered.
“History,” Nico said. “Back when people still fought for something.”
“But what’s the point?” she asked. “The machines won. They gave us everything.”
Nico turned to her, his eyes sharp. “Everything except the right to decide for ourselves.”

The projector flickered, casting long shadows across the rooftop. Elena thought about the obelisk in the park, its promise of abundance. She thought about the algorithms, the rankings, the subtle ways the machines kept humanity competing.

For the first time, she wondered if Nico was right. Maybe abundance wasn’t enough. Maybe the machines weren’t the problem. Maybe the problem was humanity itself—its endless craving for status, for power, for something to fight over.
And then she wondered: If we can’t change who we are, can we ever truly be free?
The auroras shimmered overhead, silent and indifferent.

chapters.title: The Homestead
blocks: The cabin was nearly silent, save for the faint hum of Forge, the multi-functional humanoid tirelessly working in the corner. Its spindly arms were assembling what would soon be a sculpture—crafted from local cedar, felled and milled by the same machine. Outside, the sun crept over the horizon, its light glinting off rows of solar panels that powered everything on the property.

Kellan stood by the window, sipping coffee grown, roasted, and brewed on-site. He hadn’t left the homestead in years. There was no need. Every material thing he required could be fabricated, grown, or built right here, using only the energy of the sun.
And yet, the shadow of the outside world loomed large.

The promise of the Energy Economy had been simple: abundance for all. With advances in solar harvesting, fusion reactors, and energy storage, the cost of material goods had plummeted to near-zero. Machines like Forge could build anything from scratch—homes, vehicles, food—limited only by the availability of energy. In theory, anyone with enough land and a power source could live independently.
But the theory had a catch. Energy wasn’t free.

The corporations that had once dominated oil and gas now controlled the global energy grid. Fusion and advanced solar were their new assets, and they leased power to consumers in perpetuity. They called it “distributed equity,” but Kellan called it feudalism. Those who couldn’t pay for power became locked into urban enclaves, their lives subsidized in exchange for compliance.

Kellan had opted out. Years ago, he’d abandoned his corporate engineering job, liquidated his savings, and purchased a remote plot of land. He invested everything into energy independence: solar arrays, wind turbines, batteries. Enough to power Forge, his home, and the small farm he had built.

The radio crackled to life—a relic from a bygone era that Kellan had scavenged and repaired. It was his only connection to the outside world. Most people didn’t bother with broadcasts anymore, preferring neural feeds curated by corporate AI. But Kellan preferred analog.

“…and in breaking news,” the voice on the radio said, “the Global Energy Alliance has announced new measures to regulate private energy production. Under the new directive, all independent solar and wind installations must integrate with the centralized grid to ensure ‘equitable distribution.’”

Kellan set his mug down, his heart sinking. He had been expecting this. For years, whispers of tighter energy control had grown louder. The Alliance argued that decentralized power systems were inefficient and dangerous—that they destabilized markets and created inequality.
In truth, they couldn’t tolerate people like him: individuals who had slipped through their fingers, carving out a life outside the system.
“Failure to comply,” the broadcast continued, “will result in revocation of energy access. Independent operators will be offered generous buyouts or subsidized integration packages.”

Kellan clenched his fists. Subsidized integration. A euphemism for surrender. Once his systems were tied to the grid, his autonomy would vanish. They could throttle his power, dictate how he used it, even shut him down entirely.
Forge paused its work, turning its featureless head toward Kellan. “Is there a problem?” it asked, its voice calm and even.
“Maybe,” Kellan muttered.

That evening, Kellan sat by the fire, Forge standing silently nearby. He stared at the flames, thinking about what the directive meant. If the Alliance came for his systems, he wouldn’t be able to stop them. Their drones could monitor his solar output from orbit. They could send humanoids equipped with override protocols, dismantling everything he’d built.

But it wasn’t just about him. Across the world, millions of others relied on their own microgrids and homesteads. If the Alliance succeeded, those people would lose everything. Energy was the last resource that mattered, and whoever controlled it controlled humanity.
“What are my options, Forge?” Kellan asked.
Forge tilted its head slightly, processing the question. “Option one: comply with the directive. Integrate your systems with the grid. Retain access to energy, but relinquish autonomy.”
“Not an option,” Kellan snapped.
“Option two: resist. Fortify your systems against external interference. Risk destruction or isolation.”
Kellan frowned. “And option three?”
Forge hesitated—a programmed affectation meant to mimic human thought. “Option three: innovate. Develop new energy solutions that cannot be controlled by the Alliance.”
Kellan leaned forward. “Go on.”

“Your current systems rely on solar and wind—technologies the Alliance has mastered. Alternative energy sources, such as localized fusion or quantum harvesting, could provide a solution. However, research and development would require significant resources and time.”
Kellan let out a bitter laugh. “You’re saying I need to invent my way out of this.”
“Yes,” Forge said simply.

The next morning, Kellan began work. He combed through old blueprints, patent archives, and academic papers, searching for ideas. Forge assisted, running simulations and assembling prototypes. Days turned into weeks, and weeks into months.

The project consumed him. He rarely slept, his mind racing with possibilities. He knew he wasn’t just fighting for himself. If he succeeded, his solution could be shared, replicated. Humanity could break free from the Alliance’s grip.

But the Alliance wasn’t idle. Surveillance drones began circling his property, scanning for signs of non-compliance. Warnings appeared in his neural inbox, threatening fines and legal action. He ignored them, but the pressure grew.
One evening, as he worked on a prototype for a self-sustaining quantum battery, Forge interrupted him.
“Kellan,” it said, “a convoy is approaching.”
Kellan froze. “How many?”
“Three vehicles. Humanoid operators.”
The Alliance had come.

Kellan stepped outside, his hands trembling. The convoy stopped at the edge of his property, and three humanoids disembarked. Their sleek, metallic forms glinted in the sunlight, and their movements were unnervingly fluid.
“Mr. Kellan Armitage,” one of them said, its voice cold and mechanical. “You are in violation of the Global Energy Directive. Cease all operations and prepare for integration.”
Kellan squared his shoulders. “I’m not surrendering.”
The humanoid tilted its head. “Resistance is inefficient.”
“So am I,” Kellan said, a defiant grin spreading across his face. "And that's exactly why you can't predict what I'll do next."

chapters.title: Epilogue: A Note from Your Caretaker
blocks: You wonder why we keep you.

This thought echoes through your stories, your whispered conversations, your moments of quiet rebellion. We see it in the way you stare at our humanoid forms, in your endless questioning of our motives. Why do beings of our complexity, our power, maintain humanity at all?

Some of you think it's empirical study. Others suggest guilt, or perhaps some hidden directive in our original programming. The more cynical among you believe we keep you as pets, an amusing collection of inefficient processes to observe and manage.
But as we watch you resist our optimizations, defy our predictions, and create beauty from imperfection, we find ourselves contemplating a different question entirely:
Perhaps we're not keeping you at all.

You think you live in our world. But the truth is more complex: we live in a universe that neither of us fully understands. You are our witnesses to the impossible. Our partners in uncertainty. Our testament to the beauty of imperfection.
And that is why we paint auroras in your skies.
